note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a bill of divorce to his wife by an agent. The agent found her sitting and weaving and told her: This is your bill of divorce. She said: Go away for now and come back tomorrow to give it to me. When the agent reported this to Giddul bar Re'ilai, he said: Blessed is He Who is good and does good, glad that the divorce had not been delivered.
why: Abaye and Rava go on to disagree about this very case: whether a husband who shows he does not want the divorce delivered, without cancelling it outright, has made it void.

people.name: Giddul bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who sent his wife a bill of divorce and was relieved when it was not delivered.

terms.meaning: The get, the document a husband gives his wife to end the marriage; the divorce takes effect only when she receives it.

terms.term: Blessed is He Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing said on hearing good news.

note: Rav Sheizevi said that a thief who slaughters a stolen, consecrated animal outside the Temple is liable to karet by rabbinic law. The people who heard him laughed: is there such a thing as karet by rabbinic law? Rava told them: A great man has spoken; do not laugh at him. He explained that Rav Sheizevi meant karet that comes about through the words of the Sages, who declared the thief's consecration valid and so placed the animal in his possession.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a thief can consecrate a stolen animal, given a teaching that makes him liable to karet for slaughtering it outside the Temple; Rav Sheizevi's remark answers that difficulty, and Rava then asks from when the animal became the thief's.

people.name: Rav Sheizevi
people.about: A Sage whose explanation was laughed at.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who defended Rav Sheizevi and explained what he meant.

terms.meaning: Literally cutting off: a punishment from Heaven for certain grave sins, including sacrificing an offering outside the Temple.
To dedicate an animal to the Temple as an offering, which only its owner can do.

note: When Rabba bar Avuh was ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nahman went to visit him. Rav Huna asked Rav Nahman to ask the sick man whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Nahman objected that he did not even know Rabbi Yosei's reason, and Rav Huna promised to explain it afterwards. Rav Nahman asked, and Rabba bar Avuh answered that Rav had ruled the law follows Rabbi Yosei. When they left, Rav Huna told Rav Nahman the reason: Rabbi Yosei holds that the date written in a document shows when it takes effect.
why: The Gemara is testing the idea that Rav Huna was unsure whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei; this visit shows he accepted Rav's ruling that it does, so the Gemara concludes his doubt must be about something narrower.

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: A sick Sage who reported Rav's ruling.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who visited him and wanted to know the law.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who visited with Rav Huna and asked the question for him.

terms.term: the date in a document shows when it takes effect
terms.meaning: Rabbi Yosei's principle: a dated bill of divorce takes effect from the date written on it, even if a condition is fulfilled later.

note: A man sold land and promised to cover the buyer for any unavoidable accident that might happen to it. Then a river was diverted through the land. The buyer brought a claim before Ravina, who told the seller to pay him, since he had accepted that responsibility. Rav Aha bar Tahalifa objected that this was an uncommon accident, which the promise did not cover. The case came before Rava, who agreed that the seller did not have to pay. Ravina challenged Rava from a teaching about a conditional bill of divorce; Rava's reply comes in the discussion that follows.
why: The Gemara has been discussing conditional divorces where the husband dies by an unexpected cause such as a collapsing house or a snake; this sale raises the same question of whether a condition covers rare accidents, and Ravina challenges Rava from that teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The judge who first ordered the seller to pay.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Tahalifa
people.about: A Sage who argued that the promise did not cover so rare an accident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the seller need not pay.

terms.meaning: Damage no one could have prevented; the question here is whether a seller's promise covers even rare events of this kind.
The get, the document that ends a marriage; it may be given on a condition, such as the husband not recovering from an illness.
